analysis.one_liner: Exempts tribal businesses on tribal lands from federal labor law and union protections.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 249-177 on Nov. 17, 2015, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act, the nation's main federal labor law, so that Indian tribes and any business they own and operate on tribal lands are not considered "employers" under the law. That would put tribal casinos, hotels, and other enterprises outside the National Labor Relations Board's authority, meaning workers there could not use federal processes to form unions or resolve unfair-labor-practice claims. Supporters called it a sovereignty fix, saying tribes are governments and should be treated like states, which are already exempt. Opponents said it strips union rights from tens of thousands of casino and resort workers, many of whom are not tribal members. It passed the House with strong Republican backing but received no Senate action before Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribal governments and tribally owned enterprises such as casinos and resorts, which would no longer face National Labor Relations Board elections, complaints, or union drives on their lands.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the NLRA so that any Indian tribe, or any enterprise or institution owned and operated by a tribe and located on its lands, is not considered an employer under the Act [S4][S5].

Defines covered Indian lands broadly, including all reservation lands, trust lands, and former reservation lands in Oklahoma, so the exemption reaches the full range of tribal commercial operations [S5].
Supporters argued it restores tribal sovereignty by treating tribes like state governments, which are already exempt from the National Labor Relations Act [S1][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Workers at tribal casinos, hotels, and other tribally owned businesses, who would lose federal collective bargaining rights and the ability to file unfair-labor-practice claims; many are not tribal members.
analysis.who_pays_short: Casino and resort workers on tribal lands

drawbacks.text: The bill removes National Labor Relations Act coverage from workers at tribally owned businesses, eliminating federal union formation and unfair-labor-practice protections for employees on Indian lands [S4][S5].

Opposition in the House was substantial: 177 members voted no, including 159 of 188 House Democrats, reflecting the argument that the exemption leaves a large class of casino and resort workers with no federal labor recourse [S8].

Unions and worker advocates objected that many affected workers are non-tribal members employed at commercial gaming operations, so the exemption functions less like a government exemption and more like removing labor rights from a private-sector-scale workforce (widely reported).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill poses a real trade-off rather than a clear win for either side. Tribal governments have a legitimate claim that they should not be regulated as ordinary employers on their own lands, and states enjoy exactly that exemption today. But the enterprises covered are often large commercial casinos and resorts employing thousands of people, and the bill gives their workers nothing in place of the federal protections it removes. Had it become law, the cost would have fallen on casino and resort workers, many of them non-tribal members, in the form of lost union rights.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 249-177 in November 2015, was sent to the Senate, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Introduced Jan. 22, 2015 by Rep. Todd Rokita (R-IN) with 54 cosponsors (52 Republicans, 2 Democrats) [S1][S6][S7].
The House Education and the Workforce Committee reported the bill as amended in September 2015 (H. Rept. 114-260) [S3][S7].
The House passed it Nov. 17, 2015, 249-177: 225 of 245 Republicans voted yes and 18 no; 24 of 188 Democrats voted yes and 159 no [S8].
The Senate received the bill Nov. 18, 2015 and took no further action; it died when the 114th Congress ended Jan. 3, 2017 [S5][S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers at tribal enterprises, who kept federal labor protections, and the National Labor Relations Board's authority over tribally owned casinos remained intact. Tribal governments and enterprises did not get the exemption they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Casino workers who kept union rights

for.name: Rep. Todd Rokita
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through the Education and the Workforce Committee to House passage.

for.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing and markup, ordered the bill reported amended by voice vote, and reported it Sept. 10, 2015.

against.name: Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill Nov. 18, 2015 and never took it up; no vote was ever held.

against.name: Labor unions and casino worker advocates
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, arguing it stripped union rights from thousands of casino and resort workers, many of them non-tribal members.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split mostly by party, 225 of 245 Republicans in favor versus 159 of 188 Democrats opposed, with 24 Democrats and 18 Republicans crossing party lines.

industries.industry: Tribal casinos and tribally owned resorts and enterprises
industries.note: The bill would free tribally owned commercial operations from National Labor Relations Board jurisdiction over union elections and unfair-labor-practice claims on tribal lands. Supporters framed this as an extension of tribal sovereignty over tribal lands; workers at these businesses would have lost the federal labor protections the law currently provides [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Organized labor and casino worker unions
industries.note: Unions would lose the ability to organize thousands of casino, hotel, and resort workers on tribal lands and would lose federal unfair-labor-practice remedies in that sector [S5].

Tribal casinos would operate free of the federal labor law that binds competing non-tribal casinos, giving tribally owned operations a competitive advantage in labor relations and operating conditions [S5].
